│   │   ├── serverSettingsService.ts # HTTPS, branding, backup/restore
│   │   ├── backupService.ts        # Database backup + restore. Owns the whole mechanism, extracted from serverSettings.ts (2026-08). `createBackup({password, kind, actor})` STREAMS `pg_dump` stdout → gzip → optional AES-256-GCM cipher → `data/backups/<id>`, registers the file in the `backup_history` Setting row, and returns `{record, path}` — the route streams that file to the client, so peak memory is a couple of stream watermarks instead of three copies of the dump (the prior version was `execSync` + `readFileSync` + `gzipSync` + in-memory cipher + `res.end(payload)` under a 120 s cap, which blocked the web role's event loop for the whole dump and failed or OOMed at the documented 50 GB DB sizing). `restoreBackup({filePath, password})` detects encryption from the magic header, decrypts through a stream, and wraps the psql run in the documented TimescaleDB sequence — `timescaledb_pre_restore()` / restore / `timescaledb_post_restore()` in THREE separate sessions, with post_restore in a `finally` so a failed restore can never leave the database in restoring mode (previously absent entirely, which made restores on any Timescale install unreliable). Connections ride libpq PG* env vars via `utils/pgEnv.ts`, never argv. Progress-based watchdog (`NO_OUTPUT_TIMEOUT_MS`) replaces the fixed wall-clock cap. Also owns `listBackups` / `getBackupRecord` / `deleteBackup` / `backupFilePath` (traversal-checked) / `isEncryptedBackupFile` / `timescaleInstalled`. **Post-restore the pool is recycled** (`prisma.$disconnect()` in the `finally`): `--clean --if-exists` drops and recreates every table, so connections opened beforehand hold stale relation OIDs and fail with `XX000 could not open relation with OID <n>` — the route additionally returns `restartRequired: true` and the UI shows a restart banner, because a dump from a different schema version also invalidates the running generated client and the other roles have their own pools. File format unchanged so pre-existing backups still restore: `"POLARIS␀"|salt(32)|iv(16)|authTag(16)|gzip(sql)` ciphertext.
│   │   ├── backupScheduleService.ts # Operator-configured AUTOMATIC backups (`backupSchedule` Setting; Server Settings → Maintenance → Scheduled Backups). Default `enabled:false` — many sites already back this Postgres up with an enterprise product, and an upgrade must not start writing gigabytes unasked. Shape `{enabled, intervalHours(1-168), hourUtc(0-23|null), retainCount(1-50), passphrase, copyToDir, lastRunAt, lastError}`. `isScheduledBackupDue(schedule, now)` is PURE (unit-tested): never-run ⇒ due immediately (enabling produces a recovery point now, not intervalHours later); otherwise due once intervalHours elapse since the last SUCCESS; a pinned `hourUtc` holds an otherwise-due run until that hour but runs anyway past 2× the interval so a host that was down through its window is not skipped forever. `copyBackupOffHost` copies each finished backup to a mounted share (best-effort — a full share must not fail a good backup). Passphrase masked on read / preserved on masked write like every other secret surface, and strength-checked through `utils/backupPassword.ts`.

│   │   ├── mibService.ts            # SNMP MIB module storage + minimal SMI parser. `parseMib` validates uploads (extracts moduleName + IMPORTS) on the upload hot path. `parseMibStructured` is the heavier peer used by the Browse modal + MIB-aware walk: extracts SYNTAX (with INTEGER enum value labels), MAX-ACCESS / ACCESS, STATUS, DESCRIPTION, INDEX clauses, and SEQUENCE OF table structure. Parses on demand; `oidRegistry` already keeps every MIB's contents in memory after `ensureLoaded()`. Per-asset **scoped** resolution: device-specific MIBs override vendor-wide MIBs override generic MIBs override the built-in SMI seed. │   │   ├── vendorTelemetryProfiles.ts # Per-vendor SNMP CPU/memory/temperature/disk profile registry. The constant stays as a fresh-install fallback while the DB cache warms up. Transforms from `symbolTransforms.ts` are not yet applied at sample-write time — that plumbing lands in a follow-up. Profile shape carries optional `cpu` / `memory` / `disk` / `temperature` queries — temperature is a single-scalar form for vendors whose hardware publishes one Celsius reading instead of the table-based ENTITY-SENSOR-MIB walk (consumed by `collectTemperaturesSnmp` as a third fallback after ENTITY-SENSOR-MIB + the Fortinet `fgHwSensorTable` sensor-name heuristic). Built-ins for Cisco / Juniper / Mikrotik / Fortinet FortiSwitch (matched before generic Fortinet via `model="FortiSwitch"`; CPU uses `fsSysCpuUsage` @ 12356.106.4.1.2 scalar percent; memory uses bytes form via `fsSysMemUsage` @ 12356.106.4.1.3 + `fsSysMemCapacity` @ 12356.106.4.1.4 — NOT a percent like the FortiGate variant — all three seeded into oidRegistry so the probe works without uploading FORTINET-FORTISWITCH-MIB) / Fortinet FortiAP (matched before generic Fortinet via `model="FortiAP"`; distinct OID root @ 12356.120 — FortiAPs don't expose anything under FortiGate's 12356.101 or FortiSwitch's 12356.106; CPU = `fapCpuUsage` @ 12356.120.3.41 scalar percent; memory = `fapMemoryUsage` @ 12356.120.3.42 scalar percent (single-value form like FortiGate, NOT FortiSwitch's bytes form); temperature = `fapTemperature` @ 12356.120.3.44 scalar Celsius; all three seeded into oidRegistry so the probe works without uploading FORTINET-FORTIAP-MIB) / Fortinet (SNMP path) / HP-Aruba / Dell. The FortiSwitch profile additionally carries a `model` identity query (`fsSysVersion` @ 12356.106.4.1.1, seeded) — the combined "model-firmware" string parsed by `utils/fortiswitchModel.ts`; `collectSystemInfoSnmp` reads it on the heavy pass and `recordSystemInfoResult` adopts the parsed "FortiSwitch <token>" onto `Asset.model` while the stored model is still empty or the generic "FortiSwitch…" discovery literal (edge-triggered, `asset.model_detected` Event; operator-typed models are never overwritten, and the projection's deliberate fortiswitch-model skip means discovery can't clobber it back). Not part of the editable ManufacturerProfile surface.
│   │   ├── monitorOverrideService.ts # Asset monitor-override semantics. `Asset.monitorOverride` is an **explicit operator-intent bit** — true when an operator deliberately set this asset's `monitored` state away from the discovering integration's per-class `addAsMonitored` default. It is the (monitored XOR addAsMonitored) divergence but is WRITTEN only at operator-action time; nothing re-derives it from incidental state, so incidental divergence (decommission clamp, created-before-flag-enabled, HA standby) leaves it false and self-heals. Exports: pure helpers `getAddAsMonitoredFromConfig(integrationType, integrationConfig, assetType)` (JSON-path lookup of `<klass>Monitor.addAsMonitored` per the 5-class map), `computeMonitorOverride(monitored, addAsMonitored)` (XOR), `resolveMonitorOverride(input)`, `buildMonitoredSweep(addAsMonitored, existing)` (returns `{monitored: bool}` or `{}` for discovery-side stamps, gated on the existing override flag — reads it, never writes it), `classBlockKeyForAssetType`, `snapshotAddAsMonitoredByAssetType(integrationType, integrationConfig)` (5-way snapshot used by the integration-save change detector and the preflight endpoint); plus async SQL helpers `recomputeMonitorOverrideForAssets(prisma, assetIds[])` (operator-write-path post-hook — single SQL UPDATE) and `sweepMonitoredForIntegration(prisma, integrationId)` (integration-save sweep — `monitored = addAsMonitored` for every non-override asset under this integration, scoped via the JSON path; does NOT recompute overrides — a flag flip respects pins). All SQL paths use the same `assets.config #>> '{<klass>Monitor,addAsMonitored}'` JSON-path technique the cutover migration uses — keep these in sync.
│   │   ├── monitorSettingsService.ts # Business logic for the four-tier monitor-settings hierarchy CRUD, extracted from `src/api/routes/monitorSettings.ts` (which keeps only Zod parsing + permission gates). Manual-tier Setting("manualMonitorSettings") read/upsert, integration-tier `Integration.config.monitorSettings` read/rewrite, MonitorClassOverride CRUD (Phase 2 manual-scope-only guards — integration-scoped writes 400; service-layer uniqueness for the NULL-integrationId case Postgres's @@unique can't catch), and the asset-overrides reverse lookup. `assertPollingCompatible` (source-kind matrix + per-stream STREAM_METHODS + the ICMP-only-on-response-time rule) lives here and guards integration-tier + class-override writes. Every write calls `invalidateMonitorSettingsCache` for the matching scope and logs an Event. Resolution itself stays in `monitoringService.ts` (`resolveMonitorSettings`) — this service owns only the tier CRUD.
│   │   ├── monitoringService.ts     # Authenticated response-time probes (fortimanager/fortigate/snmp/winrm/ssh/icmp) + System tab telemetry (CPU/memory) + system-info (interfaces/storage) collection. runMonitorPass dispatches all three cadences; per-stream tier-aware retention prune helpers. **Prune layer is fleet-coordinated**: `runRetentionPrune` (the single entry called from `monitorAssets`'s heavy loop) gates on a persisted `Setting("lastRetentionPruneAt")` (24h cadence, `RETENTION_PRUNE_INTERVAL_MS`) and takes a Postgres session-level advisory lock (`pg_try_advisory_lock(0x504c5253,1)` on a dedicated `getDirectDatabaseUrl()` connection) so only ONE monitor replica prunes at a time — the rest return `{skipped}`. Inside the lock it runs `pruneMonitorSamples` / `pruneTelemetrySamples` / `pruneSystemInfoSamples`, one prune per (table × tier) — detail (column `timestamp`), hourly + daily (column `bucketStart`) — with retention from `getSampleRetention()` (per-class: `default` / `switch` / `accessPoint`), then bumps the persisted timestamp. LLDP neighbors ride the systemInfo detail retention since they're current-state, not time-series. `dropChunks(cutoff)` is the O(1) pre-filter for whole aged chunks; the residue row-DELETE is compression-frontier-safe — `pruneTierByDays` routes through `tieredPruneWindow` (skips the DELETE entirely when the whole delete set is past the compress-after frontier, the common rollup case) and `pruneSelectionAwareDetail` through `unselectedSlowPruneWindow`, so a row-DELETE never decompresses a compressed chunk (prod incidents 2026-06-08, 2026-06-17). The old in-memory `lastPruneAt=0` trigger fired the prune on every process boot and, under a monitor restart loop, fanned into the 2026-06-17 hourly-table DELETE pile-up that pinned the xmin horizon. **Sample writes are async-buffered**: every `record*` function (`recordProbeResult` / `recordTelemetryResult` / `recordSystemInfoResult` / `recordFastFilteredResult`) hands sample rows to `sampleWriteBuffer.enqueue*` instead of issuing per-call `prisma.<table>.create*` — those are batched into one `createMany` per 2 s flush window. **The probe-path Asset.update (status/counters/last*At) is also buffered** via `probePatchBuffer.enqueueProbePatch` — one bulk `UPDATE … FROM (VALUES …)` per 2 s window covers every asset's state write instead of one `prisma.asset.update` per probe. The five-state machine reads its own writes via `getPendingProbePatch(assetId)`: `recordProbeResult` overlays the in-flight patch onto the loaded Asset row BEFORE computing the next state, so the threshold counters advance correctly across same-window probes. Telemetry/systemInfo cadences still issue per-asset `prisma.asset.update` for `lastTelemetryAt` / `lastSystemInfoAt` — those run on slower cadences (60 s / 600 s+) where per-tick connection pressure is much lower; if needed, the same buffer pattern applies straightforwardly. Three writes stay synchronous because they need per-asset replace semantics: the `$transaction` for `assetAssociatedIp` (delete-non-manual + createMany inside `recordSystemInfoResult`), `persistLldpNeighbors` (per-asset full-replace of the LLDP neighbor table with a 48 h stickiness grace), and `persistWirelessStations` (per-scrape full-replace of the connected-client table; no stickiness because clients are transient by design). The LLDP and wireless paths use a single bulk `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE` raw-SQL statement (plus a separate `deleteMany` for stale rows) so the connection isn't held across N pipelined updates inside a transaction — caller pre-assigns ids in JS so insert-vs-update is controlled by id collision, not by the business-key unique constraint which can't be used as a conflict target since Postgres treats NULL as distinct in unique indexes. **Probe path issues exactly one Asset findUnique** — `probeAsset(assetId, out?)` stashes its loaded asset row into the caller's optional out-object so `recordProbeResult(assetId, result, preloadedAsset?)` can skip its own findUnique on the state-machine update path. The hot loop (runProbeFor) and pg-boss probe workers both pass the out-object; the /probe-now route doesn't bother (one operator-triggered request per click). **LLDP asset match index is module-cached** with a 60 s TTL — `persistLldpNeighbors` used to call `buildLldpAssetMatchIndex` on every system-info pass (`findMany` over every Asset row plus its associatedIpRows + macAddressRows), now goes through `getLldpAssetMatchIndex()` which dedups concurrent rebuilders via an inflight Promise and returns the cached map within the TTL window. Worst-case stale-cache effect is one cycle of "LLDP neighbor matched to wrong asset" which self-corrects on the next scrape; `invalidateLldpMatchCache()` is exported for future callers that want explicit refresh after a bulk asset write. **FortiSwitch port-VLAN overlay**: in the SNMP systemInfo path on `assetType="switch"` assets with a Fortinet source AND a resolvable `controllerFortigate`, `collectSystemInfo` calls `fetchFortiswitchControllerPortsCmdb(integration, controllerName, timeoutMs)` after `collectSystemInfoSnmp` returns and overlays per-port `nativeVlan` + `taggedVlans` onto matching `InterfaceSample` rows by ifName == port-name. The fetcher hits the parent FortiGate's `/api/v2/cmdb/switch-controller/managed-switch?datasource=1` once per (integration, controller) per 30 s (`fortiswitchControllerPortsCache` mirrors the `fortinetControllerCache` TTL); the response carries every managed switch's full ports table including `vlan` / `allowed-vlans` / `untagged-vlans`, parsed via `parseFortiosVlanList` which handles FortiOS's three shapes (array of `{vlan-id}` objects, raw number array, comma+range string) and drops `"all"` placeholders. Tagged set is `allowed-vlans − untagged-vlans` so a port carrying only its native isn't duplicated as tagged. The **same CMDB fetch also carries trunk membership** (a `ports[]` entry that lists `members` IS a trunk — the auto-ISL FortiLink uplink is named after the switch serial and has exactly one member): `overlayFortiswitchTrunkMembers` stamps `ifParent=<trunk>` + `ifType="physical"` onto each member's `InterfaceSample` row (synthesizing the row when IF-MIB omitted the subordinate port) and marks the trunk row `ifType="aggregate"`, mirroring the FortiGate-side aggregate back-fill in `collectSystemInfoFortinet`. This parent/member linkage lets the topology layer (`interfaceTopologyService.preferPhysical` + the single-member swap in `topologyGraphService.ts`'s `ifDetail`) render a single-member trunk as its physical port — so the Device Map FortiLink tooltip shows the real cable port (e.g. `port52`) instead of the opaque serial-named trunk. The member-list parser (`parseFortiosMemberList`) is deliberately permissive across FortiOS shapes (array of `{member-name}`/`{q_origin_key}`/`{name}` objects, bare-string array, or space/comma string); the exact CMDB field still wants confirmation on a live FortiOS 7.x device, so the overlay is best-effort and degrades to "no trunk resolved" on an unexpected shape. Best-effort — any overlay failure leaves both VLAN fields null/empty on every row and the interface scrape proceeds. Strictly additive to the SNMP IF-MIB walk. **Interface MAC fold**: when the scrape returns interfaces, EVERY interface MAC (monitored or not) is reconciled into `AssetMacAddress` (source="monitor-interface") via `reconcileInterfaceMacs` — contiguous MACs coalesce into `[mac, macEnd]` range rows (a 48-port switch stores one row), full-replace scoped to that source only so rows owned by discovery/agent/manual writers are never touched. Gated on the scraped-MAC set being non-empty, so the no-MAC case costs zero extra round-trips.
│   │   ├── sampleWriteBuffer.ts     # Periodic batch-flush buffer for the six append-only monitor sample tables (asset_monitor_samples / asset_telemetry_samples / asset_hardware_sensor_samples / asset_interface_samples / asset_storage_samples / asset_ipsec_tunnel_samples). Per-table in-memory arrays + a 2 s `setInterval` flush + a 5,000-row size threshold for burst publishers (e.g. a manual probe-all-now). `flushTable` snapshots the array up front so concurrent enqueues during the awaited `createMany` land in a fresh buffer; on flush failure the snapshot is re-prepended for the next tick's retry. Deadlock retries go through `retryOnDeadlock` (3 attempts, 25-75 ms jitter — same as `reconcileMacAddresses`). Flush duration is observed via the existing `polaris_sample_write_duration_seconds{table}` histogram; current depth per table is exported as `polaris_sample_buffer_depth{table}`. Trade-off: up to 2 s of sample rows are lost on a hard crash — acceptable because samples are an append-only time series and the next cadence tick re-supplies fresh data. **State-side writes (Asset.monitorStatus / counters / lastMonitorAt / monitorStatusChangedAt) live in the companion `probePatchBuffer` with last-write-wins-with-stamp-preservation semantics** instead of this append-only buffer; same 2 s window but different shape because state needs replace semantics and the buffer needs to serve reads (the state machine's threshold counters require read-your-writes). `shutdownFlushSampleBuffers()` is awaited from the SIGTERM/SIGINT hook in `src/app.ts` so a graceful restart doesn't drop the in-flight buffer. **The buffer covers only the six DETAIL tables — the twelve rollup tables (`*_hourly` / `*_daily`) use `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` from `sampleRollupService.ts` instead** because rollup writes need upsert semantics (idempotent re-runs over the same window must rewrite buckets in place); the append-only buffer contract intentionally has no upsert path.
│   │   ├── probePatchBuffer.ts      # Companion to sampleWriteBuffer for the STATE-side write inside `recordProbeResult`. Replaces the per-probe `prisma.asset.update` (one Prisma pool connection per probe; the dominant remaining per-tick connection draw on the monitor hot loop at 2000+ assets) with an in-memory `Map<assetId, ProbePatch>` flushed as one bulk `UPDATE … FROM (VALUES …)` statement per 2 s window. Last-write-wins per asset within the window EXCEPT `monitorStatusChangedAt`, `lastUptimeSec`, and `lastRebootAt`, which are preserved on merge (and COALESCE'd in the flush SQL) so a transition stamp / SNMP uptime reading / reboot stamp isn't NULL-erased by a subsequent same-window probe that didn't carry one (e.g. a non-SNMP probe has no uptime). The state machine reads its own writes via `getPendingProbePatch(assetId)` — `recordProbeResult` overlays the in-flight patch onto the loaded Asset row BEFORE computing the next state, so two failed probes in the same window correctly advance `consecutiveFailures` to 2 instead of both computing it as 1 against the on-disk 0. On flush-retry-exhausted failure, the snapshot is conditionally re-prepended (only entries the buffer no longer holds — concurrent enqueues represent fresher state and win). Trade-off: up to 2 s of state writes lost on hard crash, and the `monitor.status_changed` Event / `propagateAfterStatusChange` / `triggerRetryAfterStatusChange` side effects that fire on transitions run against in-memory `(previousStatus, nextStatus)` values and don't wait for the flush — propagate/retry hooks then read the DB before the buffer lands, so their effects can lag by up to one flush window before the 60 s `dependencyReconciler` and `retryQueuedReservationPushes` ticks catch up as the sources of truth. Acceptable because the state machine is self-healing within one additional probe cycle. Exports `polaris_probe_patch_buffer_depth{table=assets:probe}` gauge + `polaris_probe_patch_write_duration_seconds` histogram. `shutdownFlushProbePatchBuffer()` awaited from the SIGTERM/SIGINT hook so a graceful restart doesn't drop in-flight state.
│   │   ├── sampleRollupService.ts   # Tiered sample-retention rollup writer. Builds twelve `INSERT...ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` statements (6 source tables × hourly + daily) that aggregate raw detail samples into per-hour and per-day rollup tables. Portable across plain Postgres + TimescaleDB via `date_trunc('hour' | 'day', ts)` — single code path on both deployments. Gauge tables (monitor, telemetry, temperature, storage) emit `sampleCount + avg/min/max` per bucket; counter tables (interface, ipsec) emit per-bucket `first/last` counter endpoints + `lastBucketSampleAt` so the read layer derives rate as `(last - first) / (lastBucketSampleAt - bucketStart in seconds)` with negative-delta-as-counter-reset behavior matching the detail-tier client-side diff. IPsec additionally counts per-status sample-bucket occurrences so the chart distinguishes flapping from steady-state. Daily reads from `*_hourly` (not detail) so the daily tick stays bounded on big fleets. Driven by `src/jobs/runSampleRollup.ts`.
│   │   ├── sampleQueryRouter.ts     # Tier router. `pickSampleTier(since, retention)` returns `{tier: "detail"|"hourly"|"daily", bucketSeconds}` based on which tier still covers the requested window. `pickSampleTierForAsset(assetId, entity, since)` is the async hot-path helper used by the six chart history endpoints — resolves the configured retention for the given entity (`assets` / `cpuMem` / `temperature` / `interfaces` / `storage` / `ipsec`) from `sampleRetentionService` and applies `pickSampleTier` (which treats `FOREVER`(-1) as full coverage, `0` as tier-off). `assetId` is retained in the signature for the forthcoming selection-aware read (unselected interfaces have no rollup beyond 24h) but isn't consulted for tier selection today.
│   │   ├── sampleHistoryService.ts  # Tier-aware readers for the six chart history endpoints. Detail tier returns raw sample columns; rollup tiers translate aggregate columns back to the source-table field names so gauge charts (monitor, telemetry, temperature, storage) render unchanged — values become bucket averages with `min*` / `max*` siblings + `sampleCount` for tooltips. Counter tables (interface, ipsec) pre-compute `inBytesPerSec` / `outBytesPerSec` / `inErrorsPerSec` / `outErrorsPerSec` (and IPsec analogs) on rollup tiers so the frontend can branch on `bucketSeconds > 0` and read rates directly instead of diffing cumulative samples.
│   │   ├── sampleRetentionService.ts # Global sample-retention policy. `Setting("sampleRetention")` holds a per-ENTITY shape `{assets|cpuMem|hardware|interfaces|storage|ipsec|perfSla|process: {detail, hourly, daily}}` (8 tiered entities × 3 tiers) PLUS a parallel FLAT dimension for tables that are current-state-with-age rather than tiered time-series, where detail/hourly/daily would be meaningless: `FLAT_RETENTION_ENTITIES` = `{appMapConnections: {days}}` (`asset_process_connections`, the Application Map socket facts). `SampleRetention` is the INTERSECTION of the two records, so `retention[tieredEntity][tier]` keeps working untouched while flat entities read `retention.appMapConnections.days`; `parseSampleRetention`/`mergeRetention` loop both lists, so a stored blob that predates a flat entity simply inherits the default on read — no migration needed. Edited from Server Settings → Retention card; consumed by the prune layer (`monitoringService.pruneXxxSamples`) and the chart tier router. Legacy class-shaped Setting values migrate forward via `migrateSampleRetentionToEntities` on first boot.
│   │   ├── capacityService.ts       # Capacity snapshot: host (cpu/ram + per-volume disk free), DB sample-table breakdown, monitoring workload + steady-state size projection, severity grading (ok/watch/amber/red). Volume scan walks every distinct filesystem Polaris/Postgres write to (app dir, state dir, backups dir, plus the PostgreSQL data directory when DB is co-located — resolved authoritatively via `SHOW data_directory`, falling back to platform-conventional paths like `/var/lib/pgsql/...` when SHOW fails because the application's DB role lacks `pg_read_all_settings`), deduped by stat.dev so single-LV installs collapse cleanly and STIG-style multi-LV layouts surface each filesystem once. `recordCapacityTransition()` compares against a stored `capacity.lastSeverity` Setting and writes one `capacity.severity_changed` Event on each transition (any direction), routed out through eventArchiveService → syslog/SFTP so an alert reaches on-call before the DB dies. Feeds the Maintenance tab Capacity card and the sidebar critical alert via the /server-settings/pg-tuning endpoint. Snapshot also carries `database.timescale: { extensionInstalled, hypertableTables[] }` and a `timescale_recommended` watch-severity reason that fires when sample tables exceed 1 GB without the extension installed; reason text adapts via `deploymentContext` heuristics (local-DB vs remote/managed, bare-metal vs container). Also carries `database.connectionPool: { currentInUse, peakObserved, prismaPoolSize, pgbossPoolSize, maxConnections }` — `currentInUse` from `pg_stat_activity` at snapshot time; `peakObserved` is a rolling high-water mark tracked in module-local memory (resets on process restart); `prismaPoolSize` and `pgbossPoolSize` are the configured Polaris pool capacities (DATABASE_POOL_SIZE / POLARIS_PGBOSS_POOL_SIZE; pgboss is null in cursor mode); `maxConnections` from `SHOW max_connections`. Drives the `db_pool_undersized` watch-severity reason that fires when peak ≥80% of the combined Polaris pool capacity; suggestion text points operators at the Capacity Advisor card for the actual recommended pool sizes. The three advisor-driven reasons — `monitor_workers_undersized` (watch — single rollup naming the worst worker gap), `max_connections_undersized` (amber — fires when the advisor recommends a higher max_connections than is currently set), and `monitor_handler_timeout_pressure` (watch — fires when observed p90 ≥ 70% of `pgboss.queue.expire_seconds` on any monitor cadence) — are populated by `getCapacitySnapshotWithAdvisor()`, the two-pass orchestrator helper that builds an initial snapshot, runs the Capacity Advisor against it, then rebuilds with the advisor's gap data in scope so the reasons fire. The legacy `pgboss_recommended` / `pgboss_overdue` / `pgboss_pending` reasons + their inline manual "Enable on next restart" buttons were folded into the Capacity Advisor's QUEUE_MODE lever and removed from this service. The local `SAMPLE_TABLES` enumeration (capacity-domain, distinct from `timescaleService.SAMPLE_TABLES`) lists all 21 tables — 7 detail + 7 hourly + 7 daily — each tagged with `(entity, tier, countKey)` for the steady-state projection. **DETAIL tiers that never compress** (retention ≤ compress-after — all detail at the 7d/7d default) are projected from a **measured uncompressed daily byte-rate** (`measureDetailDailyBytes` → median size of recent settled, uncompressed chunks ÷ span, × retention) via the pure helper `projectDetailBytes` — this captures real index + page overhead and the true pinned-interface/cadence/asset mix that the hardcoded `count × rows-per-asset-per-day × bytes/row` workload model can't see (the workload model underprojected interface detail ~33× on a real fleet: 2026-06, assumed 20 ifaces/24h-cap/395 B-row vs. 9,418 pinned interfaces/7d/~1.1 kB-on-disk-row). **Rollup tiers** (hourly/daily, mostly compressed at steady state) keep the workload model — `monitored asset count × rows-per-asset-per-day × retentionDays × bytes/row` — using the CALIBRATED `DEFAULT_BYTES_PER_ROW`. It still NEVER uses the live-measured `avgBytesPerRow` (relpages ÷ pg_stat tuples): unreliable for compressed/bloated hypertables (relpages count bloated/empty pages + compressed TOAST; swings under write load), which once produced phantom 14–218 TB steady-states. The chunk measurement instead reads only dense, settled, uncompressed chunks and takes the median (robust to a single decompression-bloated outlier). Fallback to the workload model when a detail table has no settled chunk yet (fresh install) or its retention reaches past the compress frontier. `projectSteadyStateSize` + `projectDetailBytes` are exported for the unit tests that lock this. Retention values come from `Setting("sampleRetention")` via `getSampleRetention()` (per-entity per-tier — projection reads `retention[entity][tier]`) instead of the legacy single-tier `monitor.sampleRetentionDays` etc. Snapshot also carries `database.rollupLastSuccess: { hourly, daily }` (timestamps from `Setting("sampleRollup.<tier>.lastSuccess")`) which drives the new `sample_rollup_lagging` watch reason — fires when hourly is >6 h stale or daily is >36 h stale AND any sample table has rows, catching a wedged rollup before long-range chart queries silently fall back to detail-table scans. Snapshot also carries `database.io: { trackIoTiming, measured, avgBackendsBlockedOnDisk, windowSeconds }` — measured disk-read pressure from `pg_stat_database.blk_read_time` sampled between snapshots (rate via module-local `prevDbIo`, not the cumulative counters; pure math + thresholds live in `capacityDbIo.ts`, read through the PgBouncer-aware `getDirectStatsPool()`). When `track_io_timing` is off blk_read_time stays 0 so we can't measure; the `track_io_timing_off` watch (own family `pg_io_timing`, fires only when DB > RAM) nudges the operator to enable it instead of guessing.
│   │   ├── capacityDbIo.ts           # Pure disk-read-pressure rate math, split out of capacityService so it's unit-testable without the service's heavy import graph (prisma / queueService → pg-boss optional dep). `deriveDbIoVerdict(prev, current)` turns two `pg_stat_database` readings into `{ measured, avgBackendsBlockedOnDisk, windowSeconds }`; returns measured:false on first call / window < `MIN_IO_WINDOW_MS` / counter reset (so callers never alarm on bad data). Exports the tunable thresholds `DB_IO_WATCH_BACKENDS` (0.5) + `DB_IO_WARNING_BACKENDS` (2.0) and `IO_VERDICT_STALE_MS`.
│   │   ├── capacityAdvisorService.ts # Capacity Advisor: derives recommended values for connection-pool sizes, monitor worker counts (per-cadence: probe / fastFiltered / telemetry+systemInfo / **lldp** / **storage** / floating — LLDP and Storage levers added in Phase 2 alongside the queue carve-out), queue mode (cursor ↔ pg-boss), PostgreSQL `max_connections`, and PostgreSQL tuning settings from observable workload (monitored asset count, monitored interface count, per-class FortiGate count, per-cadence pass-duration P90 read from the `polaris_monitor_work_duration_seconds` histogram, observed peak connections, host RAM). Also reads `pgboss.queue.expire_seconds` for the six monitor cadences (live from the DB, so the advisor reflects what's actually in effect — not just what `EXPIRE_BY_QUEUE` in queueService.ts would write on a fresh install); surfaces the value alongside p90 in each per-cadence worker tooltip, and rolls cadences whose p90 ≥ 70% of expire_seconds into `handlerTimeoutPressure` for the capacity reason of the same name. `buildAdvisorState(inputs)` is the pure calc; `recomputeAdvisorFromSnapshot(snap, pgTuning)` is the async wrapper that loads integration counts + cadence percentiles + applicable-asset SQL counts + queue timeouts and calls into it. Cached in module memory with a 10-min TTL refreshed by `capacityWatch` and on demand by the GET endpoint. **Advisory-only** — operator clicks Stage in the UI to write env-driven recommendations to `.env` via `setEnvVar` (restart-required to take effect). `max_connections` and PostgreSQL settings stay display-only because they require a PostgreSQL restart Polaris can't trigger. Calc chain (also covered in the plan file): `workersNeeded[c] = ceil(applicable × p90 × 1.5 / cadenceInterval)`, floored at `perCadenceFloor = clamp(ceil(monitoredAssetCount × 0.5), 4, 24)` per cadence (so 6-asset installs floor at 4, 48+-asset installs cap at 24 — the floor is a "modest burst absorber" sized to the fleet rather than a fixed 24); `floatingWorkers = max(floatingFloor, ceil(0.25 × Σ))` where `floatingFloor = clamp(ceil(monitoredAssetCount × 0.5), 4, 32)`; `prismaTarget = workerCeiling + discoveryReserve + httpOverhead`; `DATABASE_POOL_SIZE = roundUpToNearest(max(prismaTarget, current), 50)`; `POLARIS_PGBOSS_POOL_SIZE = roundUpToNearest(max(pgbossTarget, current), 50)`; `recommendedMax = roundUpToNearest(ceil((effectivePrisma + effectivePgboss) / 0.65), 50)`. Cold start substitutes `COLD_START_P90_SEC = { probe: 0.4, fastFiltered: 0.6, telemetry: 0.8, systemInfo: 1.0 }` when histogram sample count is < 100 per cadence; the UI shows a "cold-start" badge per affected row. Never recommends shrinking — `changeRequired` is true only when recommended > current. **Operator override:** the advisory-only PG-tuning levers (`work_mem` / `shared_buffers` / `effective_cache_size` / `random_page_cost`) carry an `operatorOverride` flag — true when the current value was set explicitly via `ALTER SYSTEM` (detected in `computePgTuning` via `pg_settings.sourcefile` ending in `postgresql.auto.conf`). When set, `changeRequired` is forced false (`ok=true`) and the UI renders an "Operator-set" pill instead of "Stage", because the operator deliberately overrode the heuristic — e.g. lowering `work_mem` below the `RAM/128` recommendation to stop swapping — and staging would write to `postgresql.conf`, which `postgresql.auto.conf` overrides anyway (the prior behavior nagged "Stage" forever on such a value).
│   │   ├── timescaleService.ts      # TimescaleDB detection + hypertable utilities. `detectTimescale()` runs once at startup (warmed in src/app.ts) and queries `pg_extension` + `timescaledb_information.hypertables` to populate a module-level cache; `isTimescaleAvailable()` and `isHypertable(name)` are sync getters used by the prune layer and capacityService. `dropChunks(table, olderThan)` is the chunk-granular fast path used as a pre-filter before the per-class `deleteMany` in `pruneOneTable` — no-op when the target table isn't a hypertable, so callers don't need to branch. `migrateToHypertables()` runs at boot (after detection) and idempotently converts all twenty-two managed tables — the 21 tiered sample + rollup tables plus the standalone `asset_custom_widget_samples` — to hypertables (`create_hypertable(if_not_exists => TRUE, migrate_data => TRUE)`). Source tables partition by `timestamp`; rollup tables partition by `bucketStart`. Each table gets column compression with `compress_segmentby = "assetId"` + `compress_orderby` matching the partition column, and the compression policy with the `TIMESCALE_COMPRESS_AFTER_DAYS` window (default 7). **The compression policy is only removed + re-added when the window actually changed** (`compressionPolicyMatches` introspects the existing policy's `compress_after`); an unconditional recreate every boot resets the policy's 12h `next_start`, so a frequently-restarted host (in-app updates cycle `polaris.target`) would never let it fire — the failure mode that left compression off in prod and ballooned `asset_interface_samples` to 114 GB (a single 63 GB uncompressed chunk). **After the conversion loop a self-heal pass (`compressEligibleBacklog`) immediately compresses any chunk already past its window but still uncompressed** — sequential, oldest-first, capped at 8/table/boot — so a restart-cycled host self-heals instead of accumulating uncompressed delete-churn bloat. Source tables carry a composite PK on `(id, timestamp)` and rollup tables on `(id, bucketStart)` to satisfy Timescale's "all UNIQUE/PK constraints must include the partitioning column" rule — works fine on plain Postgres too. The canonical lists are exported as `SAMPLE_TABLES` (7 sources), `ROLLUP_TABLES` (14 rollups), `STANDALONE_SAMPLE_TABLES` (detail-only, no rollups — currently just `asset_custom_widget_samples`), and `ALL_HYPERTABLE_CANDIDATES` (the union of all three); capacityService consumes the union for `database.timescale.hypertableTables` enumeration, and `tests/unit/timescaleTables.test.ts` drift-guards the lists against the rollup writer, the prune layer, and the schema.
│   │   ├── queueService.ts          # Monitor work queue mode + pg-boss runtime. Two implementations: `cursor` (default — in-process worker pool inside runMonitorPass; fits small/medium fleets fine after the Step 4a split-tick fix) and `pgboss` (durable queue with per-cadence worker pools — recommended once the fleet crosses ~500 monitored assets). Queues include `polaris-monitor-losssample` for the ICMP loss sampler (own pool via `POLARIS_MONITOR_LOSS_SAMPLE_WORKERS`, 15s job expiry, 2s polling - a sample later than its 10s cadence is worthless; deliberately absent from `FLOAT_PRIORITY` so it can never borrow the floating pool from real monitoring work). Active mode lives in `Setting.monitor.queueMode`; captured at boot via `initializeQueue()` and frozen as the running process's mode regardless of subsequent Setting writes (operator changes take effect on next restart). `startPgbossWorkers()` boots pg-boss (only when boot-time mode is `pgboss`), creates **six** queues with `policy: "singleton"` + per-asset singletonKey for natural coalescing (duplicate `(assetId, cadence)` sends while a job is queued or active are absorbed silently; different assetIds run in parallel up to `localConcurrency`), and registers worker handlers that call back into the same `runFooFor()` functions the cursor pass uses. **Phase 2 carve-out**: LLDP and Storage each get their own queue (`polaris-monitor-lldp` / `polaris-monitor-storage`) and dedicated worker pool (default 12 workers each, env `POLARIS_MONITOR_LLDP_WORKERS` / `POLARIS_MONITOR_STORAGE_WORKERS`) running `runLldpFor` / `runStorageFor`. The publisher in `monitorAssets.ts` checks `Asset.lastLldpAt + lldpIntervalSeconds` / `Asset.lastStorageAt + storageIntervalSeconds` against the per-asset resolved cadence to decide when each is due. The legacy `collectSystemInfo` still walks LLDP and storage as session-coalesced side effects when interfaces + LLDP / storage resolve to the same polling method; the dedicated queues drive their own independent cadence and `persistLldpNeighbors` / `enqueueStorageSamples` are idempotent against double-walks. Cursor-mode installs keep LLDP + Storage on the legacy systemInfo path — the dedicated queues are pg-boss-only. `publishMonitorJob(cadence, assetId, transport?)` is the publisher entry point; `monitorAssets.ts` calls it from the same two ticking loops it uses for cursor — only the dispatch differs. Worker architecture: 24 dedicated workers per queue (probe / fastFiltered / telemetry / systemInfo, configurable via `POLARIS_MONITOR_PROBE_WORKERS` / `POLARIS_MONITOR_FAST_WORKERS` / `POLARIS_MONITOR_HEAVY_WORKERS` — the heavy var sets both telemetry and systemInfo) plus a **floating worker pool** (default 32, env `POLARIS_MONITOR_FLOATING_WORKERS`) that polls all four queues in priority order via `boss.fetch()`. The floating pool flows idle capacity to wherever the backlog actually is — when telemetry is chronically backed up while fastFiltered sits empty, floating workers drain telemetry instead of slots being wasted on idle queues. Total ceiling stays at 96+32=128 (same DB pool pressure as the prior flat 32×4). Implemented in `startFloatingWorkers(boss, maxFloat)` with module-level `floatingInFlight` (soft cap counter) and `floatingLoopRunning` (shutdown signal); the loop fires per-queue `boss.fetch()` calls in `FLOAT_PRIORITY` order (probe > fastFiltered > telemetry > systemInfo), dispatches each fetched job to the matching `runFooFor()`, and explicitly calls `boss.complete(name, id)` / `boss.fail(name, id, ...)`. Singleton-key dedup at the publish layer means floating workers never collide with dedicated workers on the same `(assetId, cadence)` — pg-boss already coalesces those into a single in-flight job. `POLARIS_PGBOSS_POOL_SIZE` defaults to 20 at runtime but the Capacity Advisor now scales the **recommended** value with the configured worker count: `roundUpToNearest(max(20, ceil(workerCeiling × 0.25)), 50)` — at the 128-worker default that rounds up to 50. The pool is used only for pg-boss's internal queue mechanics (boss.fetch / boss.complete / boss.fail); a too-small pool serializes the simultaneous boss.complete() calls that fire when a heavy cadence finishes a batch of work, which the operator can then see as failed jobs and stalled queue depth. The configured count per queue plus `queue="floating"` is exposed as the `polaris_monitor_workers{queue}` gauge so operators can confirm restart-pickup without reading logs. **Stable per-worker slot IDs** are assigned via [src/utils/workerSlotPool.ts](src/utils/workerSlotPool.ts) — `probe-W01..W24`, `fast-W01..W24`, `telemetry-W01..W24`, `sysinfo-W01..W24`, `floating-F01..F32`. The slot is acquired on handler entry and released on exit (try/finally) so a slot is reused across jobs and an operator can follow one slot's lifecycle through journalctl. The pickup/finish lines emit at info level ONLY when the job payload carries `verboseDebug: true` (set by the publisher when the asset's source integration has `config.verboseLogging` on); slot bookkeeping itself runs every tick regardless. Naming convention `polaris-monitor-*`; future `polaris-discovery-*` queues should be added when discovery moves under pg-boss and worker tuning revisited together.
│   │   ├── assetSightingService.ts  # DHCP-only sighting recorder: recordSightings() batch-upserts AssetFortigateSighting rows (deduped by (assetId, fortigateDevice)); getQuarantineCandidates(assetId) returns sightings within max-age; getSightingSettings/updateSightingSettings backed by Setting key "quarantineSightingSettings". Default max-age: 180 days.
│   │   ├── assetQuarantineService.ts # FortiGate MAC quarantine push/pull. quarantineAsset()/releaseQuarantine() orchestrate per-FortiGate pushes using buildTransportForIntegration() (supports both FMG proxy/direct and standalone FortiGate). Pushes to user.quarantine.targets/<name>/macs on FortiOS. quarantineTargets JSON array tracks per-target status (synced|drift|failed). verifyAssetQuarantine() drift-checks all targets without writing. statusBeforeQuarantine preserves prior status for restore on release. Auto-quarantine fires from discovery when a quarantined asset is sighted on a new FortiGate.
│   │   ├── apiTokenService.ts       # Bearer-token auth for external callers. createToken/listTokens/revokeToken/deleteToken/verifyToken. Wire format: polaris_<32-char-base64url>. argon2id hash + tokenPrefix-indexed candidate lookup. Each token is bound to a Role at mint time (roleId); requirePermission resolves the token's role matrix like a session snapshot. integrationIds required when the role grants assetsQuarantine >= write. Admin-equivalent binding logs an api_token.admin_equivalent warning Event. lastUsedAt/lastUsedIp bumped on successful verify.
│   │   ├── agentInstallService.ts   # Polaris Agent remote install/upgrade/uninstall over SSH (SFTP push + installer script) / WinRM (cert-pinned HTTPS binary pull + PowerShell). State machine pending→uploading→enrolling→active. The install-method variant (ManagedAgent.installScriptId) selects which script `installerScript`/`uninstallerScript` upload; `runInstall` re-validates the OS-lock via resolveInstallScriptId before executing. See ARCHITECTURE.md → Monitoring Architecture.
│   │   ├── agentInstallScripts.ts   # Curated catalog of agent install-method VARIANTS (metadata only: id/osPlatform/label/description/isDefault — one vetted variant per OS today: linux-systemd / darwin-launchd / windows-service). `resolveInstallScriptId(os, scriptId?)` is the server-side OS-LOCK (throws when a variant's OS ≠ the target's, or on unknown id; returns the per-OS default when none picked). Script BODIES stay inline in agentInstallService.ts (version-coupled to the binary); this module owns the picker vocabulary + validation. │   │   ├── windowsSshOnboardingService.ts # "Windows SSH Deployment" card (Integrations → Polaris Agent). Generates the ed25519 deployment keypair via ssh2's `utils.generateKeyPairSync` (OpenSSH private-key format, exactly what ssh2.connect accepts — no conversion, no shelling out), owns the Polaris-managed `ssh` Credential that holds it, and persists the card's non-secret config in the `windowsSshOnboarding` Setting. Private half is written into Credential.config (sealed at rest by db.ts) and NEVER returned by any read path — the VAPID precedent; only the public half + `SHA256:` fingerprint come out. Rotation REPLACES the credential config rather than going through updateCredential(), because mergeConfigPreservingSecrets reads an empty string as "keep the stored secret" and so cannot clear a stale `password`. `credential.ssh_keypair_generated` is stamped at WARNING level: rotating locks Polaris out of every endpoint until the onboarding script re-runs.
│   │   ├── intunePublishService.ts # Publishes the WINDOWS SSH onboarding pair to Intune as a Remediation (deviceHealthScript). Upserts by displayName (paged, bounded) so re-publishing updates one policy instead of accumulating duplicates. **NEVER calls /assign** — that is the human review gate for a script granting fleet-wide administrative SSH, and two tests pin it. The Graph API version is PROBED at first use (v1.0 then beta, cached per process): a 404 means wrong version, a 403 means the endpoint EXISTS and permission is missing, so that base is the right one. Opt-in per integration via `EntraIdConfig.publishToIntune`, which needs the Graph application permission DeviceManagementConfiguration.ReadWrite.All + admin consent. Audits `intune.script_published` at warning level.
│   │   ├── arcPublishService.ts    # Runs the SSH onboarding script on Azure Arc machines via Run Command (azureArcService.dispatchRunCommand). The Arc counterpart to intunePublishService, shaped differently because Arc has NO inert state — a run command EXECUTES on creation, so the review gate is the operator's explicit target selection rather than assignment; there is deliberately no 'all machines' affordance and ids are re-resolved against the LIVE roster (the subscription/resourceGroup/region reaching ARM come from Azure, not a request body). Sends BOTH platform scripts so each machine gets the one matching its osType; capped at 200 targets per run. Opt-in per integration via `AzureArcConfig.allowRunCommand`, which needs an Azure RBAC role carrying Microsoft.HybridCompute/machines/runCommands/write — a role ASSIGNMENT, not a Graph permission. Audits one warning-level `arc.run_command_executed` per batch with the per-machine roll-up. This is what covers Linux and Windows Server, which Intune does not reach.
│   │   ├── sshHostKeyService.ts     # Trust-on-first-use pinning for SSH SERVER host keys (`SshHostKey` table, one row per dialed host:port). `verifyOrPin` = no pin → store + accept (`ssh.host_key.pinned`); match → accept + hourly-throttled `lastSeen`; DIFFERS → refuse + warn-level `ssh.host_key.mismatch` carrying both fingerprints. Fingerprints are `SHA256:<unpadded base64>` — byte-identical to `ssh-keygen -lf` so operators can compare by eye. Opt-in per credential via `SshConfig.verifyHostKey` (default OFF, mirroring WinRM's `verifyTls`), because before this Polaris passed NO `hostVerifier` and accepted any host key on every SSH path. Lookup is served from a module-level Map (the `bumpRoleVersion` cache shape) since `withSshClient` runs on the per-minute agentless-processes cadence. `deleteHostKey` is the audited recovery for a legitimately rebuilt host.
│   │   ├── sshOnboardingScript.ts   # Pure generator for the SSH onboarding scripts, TWO PER PLATFORM. **Windows**: `buildWindowsOnboardingScript` (REMEDIATION — installs the OpenSSH Server capability, starts sshd, optionally creates the local admin account, writes the public key to %ProgramData%\ssh\administrators_authorized_keys with the Administrators+SYSTEM ACL sshd demands, optionally scopes inbound TCP/22) + `buildWindowsOnboardingDetectionScript`. **Linux**: `buildLinuxOnboardingScript` (writes the key into the USER's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys at 700/600 with correct ownership, `restorecon`s the SELinux context, and installs a **NOPASSWD sudoers drop-in** at /etc/sudoers.d/polaris-agent — validated with `visudo -cf` BEFORE install, since a malformed drop-in locks sudo out for every user on the host; deliberately does NOT install openssh-server, which would need distro-specific package management) + `buildLinuxOnboardingDetectionScript`, which unlike the Windows one ALSO checks the account and the sudoers drop-in, because both are prerequisites the agent install genuinely fails without. Each platform's key-presence predicate is emitted into BOTH its scripts from one constant so detection can never drift from what remediation writes. Emitted scripts are idempotent and delivery-neutral. `assertValidUsername` / `assertValidLinuxUsername` (stricter: POSIX charset, no DOMAIN\user) / `assertValidPublicKey` / `assertValidServerIp` are hard REJECTS, not escapes — these values are interpolated into a script an admin runs fleet-wide as root/SYSTEM.

│   │   ├── agentSigningService.ts   # Azure Trusted Signing of the Windows agent binaries (jsign via `java -jar`, token via env — never argv). Bounded for interactive use: 3h window + 250-asset deterministic sample, widened once to 48h/100 assets ONLY when the recent window is empty so a slow cadence can't read as "this hardware has no sensors". `dimensionPickerMeta()` is merged into GET /automations/schema as `dimensionPickers`.
│   │   ├── notificationEngine.ts     # The rule evaluator (run by the evaluateNotificationRules job). Threshold/state path: batch-loads in-scope assets + latest sample readings (per-metric resolvers over the sample tables; rate metrics via two-sample counter delta; `probeLossPct` = failed-probe ratio over the window via one grouped aggregate on `asset_monitor_samples`, the same computation as the dashboard Packet Loss widget — works for ANY monitored asset, not just SD-WAN — and gated to devices that are currently ANSWERING (`assetIsAnsweringProbes`: monitorStatus up/warning only, filtered inside the resolver so the composite path + preview inherit it), with a live loss alert on an asset that stopped answering CLEARED as a handoff to asset-down (`system:device-down`) rather than frozen; its `windowSec` is used EXACTLY (5-min floor, 15-min default via PROBE_LOSS_MIN/DEFAULT_WINDOW_SEC) instead of `max(windowSec, DEFAULT_LOOKBACK)`, because for a windowed ratio the window IS the measurement — the wizard calls it History — business rule 29), compares, drives the NotificationRuleState machine (clear→pending→firing) with forDurationSec + cooldown + per-rule v2 `reset` semantics (normalizeRuleToV2): manual re-arm, timed afterSec sweep, auto with optional hysteresis clearThreshold (recovery requires crossing the CLEAR line — the band between clear and fire thresholds holds the alert firing so it can't flap; a BANDED alert held in the dead band eases to its base severity instead of parking at the last band) + clear-sustain sustainSec (recovery must hold that long, tracked on NotificationRuleState.recoveredSince — transition-only writes, cancelled on re-meet/dead-band). ifOperStatus/ifAdminStatus readings are restricted to PINNED interfaces (`Asset.monitoredInterfaces`, the Down Interfaces widget's join) and ifOperStatus additionally requires admin-up — unpinned/unplugged and deliberately-disabled ports never alert. A vanished-state sweep (`clearVanishedStates`, both evaluators) clears firing/pending rows whose asset left the scope or whose dimension stopped being reported (`system:out-of-scope` / Event `notification.out_of_scope`); suppressed assets and in-scope assets with no readings at all stay frozen. Event-tail path: consumes new Event rows since a stored cursor, matches event/change rules (glob over action + level + detailsMatch), enforces cooldownSec against recent Notification rows keyed (rule, assetId-or-resourceName) with in-batch self-dedupe, inserts notifications; a companion per-tick pass (`runEventRuleTimedClear`) clears timed-reset event/change notifications after afterSec — they have no state rows, so the regular timed sweeps never see them. State writes only on transition (capacityWatch-style). All templating (messageTemplate + email composition) renders through src/utils/notificationTemplate.ts; on fire, rules with emailComposition/escalation (or {asset.*} tokens) fetch asset detail via the per-tick `assetDetail` cache (SCOPE_SELECT stays tight), snapshot the token context onto Notification.templateCtx, and `buildComposedEmail(comp, ctx)` (exported; also used by the escalation sweep + preview) renders the outbound email passed to expandDeliveries. `previewRule(input)` dry-runs a draft (builder Test, no writes; scope-only drafts list matched devices; hysteresis drafts get per-match wouldClear/inDeadBand; returns `emailPreview` when the draft has emailComposition). Pure helpers `compareNum`/`compareValue`/`globToRegExp`/`readingMeets`/`recoveredMeets` unit-tested.
│   │   ├── notificationChangeEvents.ts # Bridge from the current-state persist* functions (LLDP/processes/SD-WAN/MCLAG) to the engine's event path. `maybeEmitChangeEvents(action, assetId, name, items)` writes one audit Event per diffed change IF a change rule subscribes (via isChangeActionSubscribed) — zero cost otherwise. The engine's event-tail then turns matching events into notifications.
│   │   ├── regionScopeService.ts     # Shared effective-region/other-tag resolver — union(role, user, group). `resolveTagScopesForUser(u)` (used by GET /auth/me) + `getEffectiveRegionTags(userId)` (used by the notifications region-scoped list). Group-derived tags re-resolved live from ssoGroups.
│   │   ├── notificationRecipientService.ts # Delivery routing: `resolveRecipientUsers(tags)` / `resolveRecipientUsersByIds(ids)` (individual-account recipients) / `resolveEmailRecipients({recipientUserIds?, addresses?})` (cc/bcc + escalation-tier address resolution) / `listRecipientUsers()` (rule-builder picker) / `scopeRegionTagsOf(scope)` / pure `dedupeEmailRecipients(to, cc, bcc)` (To wins over Cc; Bcc drops anything visible) + `expandDeliveries(notificationId, targets, opts {scopeRegionTags?, assetRegionTags?, composedEmail?, escalation?})` (resolves each target's NotificationChannel, fans out into concrete NotificationDelivery rows — for email/web_push the recipients = chosen user accounts ∪ device-region users (recipientDeviceRegion × the TRIGGERING asset's stripped region snapshot: `regionSnapshot(reading.tags)` from the engine, `Notification.regionTags` from the sweep) ∪ scope-region users ∪ legacy-tag users, plus custom email addresses; with a ComposedEmail, each email target gets ONE row whose meta snapshots {composed, to, cc, bcc, subject, text, html?}; slack/teams/pushbullet get one fixed-destination row — snapshotted at fire time). Short-TTL user-tag index cache. Also home of `buildComposedEmail(comp, ctx)` (moved from the engine so the action layer can compose without a circular import; the engine re-exports it).
│   │   ├── notificationAckService.ts # One-click acknowledge links: `mintAckTokens(reqs[])` (batched createMany at delivery fan-out — one token per (notification, user, channel), NEVER a create per recipient), `inspectAckToken(raw)` (non-mutating, backs the inert GET), `redeemAckToken(raw, note?)` (re-checks alerts:write live, calls acknowledgeNotifications with `source`, spends the token), the pure `classifyAckToken(row, notif, canAck, now)` state machine (valid | already | expired | used | unknown | forbidden | cleared — `already` outranks every failure, because the clicker's intent is satisfied either way), `userCanAcknowledge(userId)` and `pruneAckTokens()` (swept hourly from the deliverNotifications tick). │   │   ├── alertBrandService.ts   # The install's letterhead in the top-right corner of an alert email — logo, application name, subtitle. `buildAlertBrandBlock()` is the whole delivery-time step: read branding once, load the mark, render both bodies + the inline attachment; memoized 60s because every email in a drain wants the identical block. `{brand.header}` is a DEFERRED token like `{chart.*}` (the logo rides as an inline CID attachment — no remote images, and Gmail/Outlook drop data: URIs — which one context string cannot carry, and deferring also means an escalation sent at T+90min carries the CURRENT branding rather than a fire-time snapshot). Artwork follows business rule 27 rather than picking a file: the email card is white, so the LIGHT-inked `polaris-horiz-light.png` wordmark is the shipped choice, and because that art already spells the product name the app name is NOT printed beside it (rule 27's showName=false); an operator's own logo gets the name as its caption plus the `renderAccentedLogo("light")` composite when they enabled an accent. The subtitle renders either way — it is the operator's own copy, not a caption for the mark. Pure pieces the tests drive: `renderBrandBlock(parts,{html})`, `fitLogo(size)` (aspect-preserving fit into 150×46, never enlarging — an unconstrained 900px banner would squeeze the headline into a two-word column), `brandTokensIn`, `substituteBrandTokens`. Every failure rung drops the logo, then the block, and the email still sends: letterhead must never be the reason an alert does not arrive.
│   │   ├── alertChartService.ts   # The last-hour hardware-sensor / CPU / memory / response-time charts embedded in an alert email. `buildAlertCharts(assetId, tokens, {now?, thresholds?})` reads the window from AssetTelemetrySample (cpuPct; memPct else memUsedBytes/memTotalBytes) + AssetMonitorSample (responseTimeMs, SUCCESSFUL probes only — plotting a failed probe as 0 would draw a fast device instead of an unreachable one), renders via utils/sparklineSvg, and rasterizes to PNG with @resvg/resvg-js (lazy import, already a dependency via appIconService). `chartTokensIn(...)` finds which {chart.*} tokens a body references; `substituteChartTokens(body, charts, {html})` swaps them for an inline `<img src="cid:…">` (HTML) or the now/avg/peak sentence (text); `attachmentsFor` returns only the images the final body cites. Built at DELIVERY time, not fire time — the drain is off the engine hot path, and an escalation at T+90min then charts the last hour as of sending rather than re-rendering a frozen snapshot. Every failure path (no samples, unreadable asset, missing native binding) degrades to the text summary: an alert must never fail to send because a chart did not draw. Packet loss is the one DERIVED series: `loadProbeLoss` buckets the probe success/failure rows into 2-minute windows and plots the failure ratio, skipping empty buckets rather than plotting a polling gap as perfect health. `chartTokenForMetric` maps the fired metric to the chart that explains it and answers for the asset_state fields too (`monitorStatus` / `consecutiveFailures` → the response-time chart, since a down device's story is the climb before it stopped answering). `isPortScopedAlert(metric)` / `PORT_SCOPED_METRICS` is the OPPOSITE decision: an alert on `ifOperStatus` / `ifAdminStatus` / `poeStatus` gets NO charts at all (empty map, zero queries), because a switch with a dead port is answering probes — that is how Polaris knows the port is down — so all four device series are flat and healthy and burying the finding. Only the interface STATE trio, deliberately: an `ifInErrorRate` / `ifOutBps` alert plausibly correlates with device load and keeps its graphs. What replaces them is alertInterfaceService's LLDP block.
│   │   ├── alertInterfaceService.ts # The per-INTERFACE facts an alert email carries when the thing that broke is one port — what the charts are replaced by (see alertChartService's `isPortScopedAlert`). `buildInterfaceLldpBlocks(assetId, metric, dimension)` is the whole delivery-time step: it returns `{html:"", text:""}` without querying unless the metric is interface-dimensioned (`INTERFACE_DIMENSION_METRICS` — the state trio plus the four counter rates, all keyed on ifName by their engine resolvers), then reads `AssetLldpNeighbor` for the port ONCE and renders both bodies from it. Two things make it work: (a) `persistLldpNeighbors` holds a vanished neighbour for a 48-hour STICKY window before deleting it, so a dead port's neighbour is still in the table at delivery — which is also why every entry prints "Last advertised", since the row predates the outage by definition and how stale it is IS the finding; (b) the port lookup is widened through `fortiapInterfaceAliases`, because a FortiAP's rows are normalized to whichever of lan1/eth0 its interface inventory reports (a switch port's alias set is just itself). `renderInterfaceLldp` emits a COMPLETE `<tr>` with its own heading or the empty string, so nothing needs a pruning pass of its own; the text form deliberately uses NO colons, because `pruneEmptyTextLines` deletes any "Label:" line with nothing after it and "LLDP neighbor on port2:" matches that shape exactly. A failed read logs and yields nothing — an alert must never fail to send because the LLDP lookup did.
│   │   ├── automationTestService.ts # Backs the wizard's Summary-step "Test delivery" buttons (`POST /automations/test-delivery`). `runTestDelivery({rule, path, mode, target, assetId?, actorUserId, actorUsername})` creates a REAL alert and dispatches ONE action of the draft — saved or unsaved — through the normal delivery path, then reports per-recipient outcomes + how many acknowledge links were minted. Deterministic node ids (asset:<id>, proc:<assetId>:<b64url(name)>, ip:<ip>, ipgroup:<cidr>) so ApplicationMapLayout blobs survive refresh. Asset nodes carry deviceIconService iconUrls. │   │   ├── appMapDiscoveryService.ts # Service & process DISCOVERY RULES (list UI on Integrations → Polaris Agent; formerly the Application Map's "Discovery" modal) + the scope-driven process/service aggregate behind the wizard. `Setting("appMapAutoMap")` = `{version:2, rules:[{id, name, enabled, mode, source, scope, assetIds, processes:{names,patterns,regex}, services:{…}}]}`. `mode`: "map" pins the Application Map surfaces AND the monitor surfaces (mapping implies monitoring); "monitor" pins ONLY monitoredProcesses/monitoredServices (pre-mode rules normalize to "map"). `source`: "manual" (wizard-authored) vs "auto" — auto rules are minted/consolidated by `recordOperatorPinChanges` (the assets-PUT pin-diff hook): one single-item rule per (item, kind, mode) with `scope:null` + explicit `assetIds` (union semantics with scope; null scope + assetIds = JUST those assets — MaintenanceSchedule precedent); the same item pinned on another asset joins the existing auto rule, un-ticking removes the asset, and an auto rule losing its LAST asset is DELETED (must never decay into a null-scope match-everything rule). Manual rules are never consolidated or trimmed by the hook; the wizard flips an edited auto rule to manual. The hook is serialized through an in-process promise chain (Setting read-modify-write isn't atomic; browser PUTs all land on the web role), never throws into the asset save, inline-applies just the touched rules, and is audited `application_map.autorule.synced`. The pure `applyPinChangesToConfig` is the unit-tested core; `resolveRuleAssetLabels` resolves every rule's assetIds to hostnames for the GET's `assetLabels`. MANY rules on purpose: a single fleet-wide selection could only express "every asset reporting this program", which over-pins — mapping `truckscale.service` for three truckscale hosts also hit every other host running it. Each rule carries its own asset scope (a `tagAssignmentService` `TagCriteria`; null = every monitored asset), so the same unit can be mapped in one part of the fleet and left alone in another; when several rules match one asset their pins UNION. `normalizeConfig` folds the PRE-RULES single-selection shape forward into one "Imported selection" rule at read time (no migration job — same trick as the flat retention default), and enforces unique rule names (case-insensitive) + ids, ≤200 rules (raised from 50 when single-item auto rules landed); `normalizeRule` enforces the 64-entry-per-array cap matching the assets PUT, case-insensitive dedup keeping the FIRST spelling (pins match inventory case-sensitively; assetIds dedup case-SENSITIVELY, cap 1000), and compiles patterns at save so a bad regex is a 400 not a silent no-match. `getInventoryAggregate(scope)` is what makes the picker granular — bounded GROUP BYs over `asset_processes`/`asset_services` joined to `assets` on `monitored=true`, narrowed to the scope's asset ids (LIMIT 2000), plus `unnest(mappedProcesses|mappedServices)` GROUP BYs for the fleet-wide already-pinned count; never load per-asset rows to count them (~400k at 2000 hosts). `PROCESS_CAPABLE_ASSET_TYPES` (`workstation`, `server` — `server` covers vCenter VMs; ESXi `hypervisor` excluded, no agent runs there) bounds EVERY candidate query (inventory aggregate, `previewScope`, apply): inventory only comes from the agent / agentless SSH+WinRM, so counting firewalls, switches, APs and printers made the device count promise pins that could never land. Deliberately NOT applied to `pinnedCounts`, which must surface a hand-applied pin wherever it lives so Unmap-everywhere means everywhere. Widening that one constant is the switch for "processes on network hardware" later. The aggregates use `COUNT(*)` not `COUNT(DISTINCT assetId)` — both tables are unique on `(assetId, name|unit)` so they're equivalent, and the DISTINCT cost a sort/hash per group over the whole table; no index on name/unit is added because both are delete-replaced per asset per scrape, so it would tax every write fleet-wide to speed one wizard step. `previewScope(scope, assetIds)` backs the wizard's device step (same union semantics as apply). `resolveBlockPins` is the PURE resolver (exact names ∪ wildcard/regex patterns). **Mapping implies monitoring, one-way:** `computePending` keeps per-surface want-sets — map wants from "map"-mode rules only, monitor wants from EVERY rule — so a map rule also pins `monitoredProcesses` / `monitoredServices` (an operator who puts a service on the map wants its telemetry), computed against the full want-set so an already-mapped-but-unmonitored item catches up; the reverse never holds, so no monitor pin ever produces a map pin, and a "monitor"-mode rule never touches a map pin. Reported as `monitorPins` on the preview + apply results. `applyRules` is STRICTLY ADDITIVE — resolves each rule's target set (scope ∪ assetIds) once, loads the inventory for the UNION of in-scope assets a single time, evaluates every rule in memory, then writes pins = union(existing, computed) in chunked Promise.allSettled batches of 50, skipping assets with nothing fresh so a repeat tick is silent; removing an item or disabling a rule stops FUTURE pinning and never retroactively unpins, because the pin arrays are operator-owned. `unmapEverywhere(kind,name)` is the separate subtractive path (strips the pin fleet-wide, deletes matching AssetProcessConnection rows, removes the name from every MAP-mode rule so the reconciler can't re-add it — monitor-only rules keep theirs — and prunes auto rules the removal emptied). `reconcileAutoMap` is the entry point for the 30-min `reconcileAppMapAutoMap` job — the "and future assets" mechanism.

│   │   ├── interfaceInventoryService.ts # CURRENT-STATE interface inventory writer (`AssetInterface`). `persistInterfaces(assetId, InterfaceSample[], now?)` maps the collector shape onto the table's 22 columns and delegates to `persistInterfaceRows(assetId, rows, now?)`, which is the core: dedupe-by-ifName (keeping the first occurrence — `(assetId, ifName)` is UNIQUE, so a device reporting a name twice would otherwise abort the whole scrape) + a 2000-row cap, both WARNED not silent, then delete-then-createMany in ONE `$transaction` so a concurrent reader sees the old set or the new set but never an empty intermediate (this table backs the System tab; an empty read renders as "no interfaces"). `firstSeen` is carried forward for a name still present and resets when one disappears and returns. `persistInterfaceRows` is exported so the agent push can reuse the rows it already built for the sample write instead of re-mapping 22 fields a second time. `dedupeAndCapInterfaces` + `INTERFACE_ROW_CAP` are exported pure for unit testing. **Callers must not invoke this from the fast pinned re-walk** — see the AssetInterface domain-model entry.
│   │   ├── interfaceTopologyService.ts # Inter-Fortinet topology inference from interface naming conventions. inferInterfaceTopology(seedAssetIds) reads the seed set's interfaces from the CURRENT-STATE `AssetInterface` table (one row per (assetId, ifName) by construction — a plain indexed read), bounded by a 1-hour `lastSeen` staleness filter so interfaces that stopped reporting don't draw edges. The cutover also FIXED a silent correctness bug: the fast pinned re-walk writes ifType/ifParent as NULL and DISTINCT ON took the newest row, so on a pinned aggregate the physical-member map saw nulls and lost it; the current-state table is written only by the full pass, which always populates them. It parses each ifName through fortinetSerialPattern, and resolves matches against the in-memory Fortinet asset inventory by serial-fragment endsWith (FortiOS-auto peer aggregates) or hostname exact/prefix-with-separator (operator-named MCLAG aggregates). Skips ambiguous (>1 hit) and self-loop matches. Returned edge ifNames prefer the underlying physical member when the matched aggregate has exactly one physical child (ifType="physical" + ifParent=aggregate) — operators trace cables by physical port, not by the FortiOS-stamped peer-named aggregate label; multi-member aggregates keep the aggregate name as the safe fallback (no single "the physical port" exists, and a comma-joined list would lie about the strict one-port-per-physical-link model). The aggregate name is still the inference SIGNAL (peer identity is encoded in it) — only the display ifName on the returned edge is normalized. Returns sibling edges plus a remoteAssets map for cross-site peers. Read-only — uses data the monitoring pipeline already collected, no new device queries. Wired into GET /map/sites/:id/topology AND `dependencyTreeService.recomputeDependencyTree` (Phase 12 of FMG/FortiGate sync) — the 1-hour window keeps that recompute under a second instead of blocking discovery for ~20 minutes.
│   │   ├── dependencyTreeService.ts # Dependency-aware monitoring suppression. recomputeDependencyTree(integrationId?) walks fortinetTopology.controllerFortigate / parentSwitch + interfaceTopologyService edges + AssetLldpNeighbor.matchedAssetId into a parent→child DAG, prunes via **physical-first** BFS layer assignment from each FortiGate (layer 1) outward — interface + LLDP edges form the primary adjacency, controller edges are a fallback for assets the physical pass didn't reach, with simple-path detection so a 3+ switch daisy chain that's only LLDP-visible between siblings (not back to the FortiGate) still chains correctly instead of collapsing every switch into a same-layer sibling of the FortiGate. MCLAG pairs and any branching / cycled controller-only component still attach as siblings. Wireless attachments override the controller signal: a **mesh-leaf AP** (seen as a station on its root AP, from `AssetWirelessStation`, or classified `meshUplink="mesh"` on its own `fortinetTopology`) depends on the root AP, and a **FortiLink switch bridged behind a FortiAP** (an AP↔switch `AssetLldpNeighbor` adjacency where the switch is not the AP's controller parent — or where the AP is a mesh leaf, whose wired LLDP adjacency is always bridged-behind) depends on that AP — in both cases the leaf's backwards controller edge is suppressed and a `mesh`/LLDP edge takes its place. Kept edges prefer the most-physical `detectedVia` (mesh > interface > lldp > controller) for the audit-trail row, persists the resulting source="computed" rows in AssetDependencyParent and Asset.dependencyLayer per scope. Operator overrides (source="override") take precedence per asset; computed rows survive alongside for audit. reconcileDependencySuppression() is the 60s reconciler — source of truth for Asset.dependencySuppressed; "all-down" multi-parent semantics (a switch with redundant uplinks suppresses only when EVERY effective parent is down or itself suppressed). Unmonitored parents are transparent — the walk continues to their grandparents. propagateAfterStatusChange(assetId) is the latency-optimization hook fired from recordProbeResult on the confirmed up/down edge only (the monitor.status_changed Event also covers the →warning edge, but propagate does not). **The ENDPOINT half (2026-08)**: `syncEndpointDependencyEdges(infra, layers)` hangs every asset whose type is NOT firewall/switch/access_point off that infra tree as a leaf, with `source="endpoint"` and at most ONE parent, resolved most-specific-first by `buildEndpointDependencyEdges` — `Asset.lastSeenSwitch` (`detectedVia="switch-port"`) → `Asset.lastSeenAp` (`"wireless"`) → the freshest `AssetFortigateSighting.fortigateDevice` that resolves to a firewall (`"sighting"`). It exists because the tree was infra-only and "no parents" means "never suppressed": a camera-station server behind a dead FortiGate alerted as plain Down while every switch and AP behind that same gate correctly read "Dep. Down". One parent rather than a union of everything that resolves, because all-down semantics model REDUNDANT parents while a switch and its gate are in SERIES — listing both would let a dead access switch under a healthy gate satisfy "some parent is ok" and keep the endpoint alerting; the series behavior instead comes from the switch itself being suppressed by its gate, and an unmonitored intermediate stays transparent so gate state still decides. Assets already carrying a `source="vcenter"` row are skipped (the hypervisor placement is the more specific truth, and unioning would break vMotion-safe cluster suppression). The pass is fleet-wide and deliberately NOT narrowed by `integrationId` — most endpoints belong to an AD/Entra/vCenter integration that never calls the recompute — and DIFFS its writes (insert missing / delete gone / retype a changed detectedVia / stamp `dependencyLayer` = parent + 1 only where it differs) instead of delete-replacing, so a steady fleet writes zero rows per discovery finalize and two integrations finalizing at once can't churn each other. Its failures are caught and logged: the endpoint half can never fail the infra recompute. Pure helpers (buildDependencyEdgesFromInputs, assignLayers, evaluateSuppression, switchNameFromLastSeenSwitch, resolveEndpointParent, buildEndpointDependencyEdges) are exported for unit testing.
│   │   ├── mapRegionService.ts      # Device Map regions: operator-drawn polygons stored as a JSON blob in Setting under key `mapRegions` (allocationTemplateService pattern). Each region carries a unique name; firewalls whose lat/lng falls inside the polygon — and FortiSwitches / FortiAPs whose `fortinetTopology.controllerFortigate` matches one of those firewalls — get tagged with `region:<name>`. **`Subnet` rows carry the tag too**: a subnet whose `fortigateDevice` matches an enclosed gate (same `controllerIdentityKeys` set) inherits the region, which is what gives the IPAM Networks list (Sources column = `fortigateDevice`) a region to filter on. `computeMembership` returns `{assetIds, subnetIds}` and the tag primitives come in pairs (`addTagToAssets`/`addTagToSubnets`, `removeTagFromAllAssets`/`removeTagFromAllSubnets`); `ReconcileSummary` counts the two populations separately (`added`/`removed`/`assetsTouched` vs `subnetsAdded`/`subnetsRemoved`/`subnetsTouched`). The reconciler **re-evaluates membership in both directions, bounded by provenance**: every add records a `RegionTagAssignment` row (one per (region, target) pair the service itself tagged — the `TagAutoAssignment` pattern, keyed by region id so a rename doesn't disturb it, with a `targetType` because subnets are targets too), and the strip half removes the tag only from recorded pairs that have drifted out of membership (`diffRegionMembership`, pure). A device that moves — a re-pinned gate, a switch repointed to another controller, a subnet re-served by a different gate — loses the tag on the next reconcile; a hand-applied tag (no provenance row, which also covers tags predating provenance) is never touched. Manually *removing* a tag from an in-polygon asset will be re-added on the next reconcile. Rename/delete keep their wholesale strips (`removeTagFromAllAssets`/`removeTagFromAllSubnets`); delete also clears the region's provenance. Region creation upserts a `Tag` registry row at `region:<name>` under category "Map Regions" so it shows up in the asset edit modal's tag picker; rename rotates the registry row; delete removes it. Fired from CRUD endpoints (await), end-of-FMG/FortiGate `syncDhcpSubnets` Phase 13, and a 6h periodic safety-net job. Membership is computed by `pointInPolygon` from `src/utils/geo.ts`; only firewalls have lat/lng so endpoints are never auto-tagged.

A `Tag.criteria` JSON blob (`{version, match:"all", rules:[...]}`, rules ANDed, values ORed) auto-applies / removes the tag on assets matching manufacturer / model / os / osVersion / hostname / department / location (exact|contains|pattern) + assetType / status (exact) + subnet (inCidr).
